So, now a natural question is, can we do something clever about using different length
encodings for different letters, so that more frequent letters get sent with shorter end codes.
So, can we optimize the amount of data we actually transfer in order to send a message
from one place to another. So, this brings us to the idea of having a variable length encoding,
where we use different strings of different lengths for different letters in the alphabet.
So, one of the most famous examples of a variable length encoding is the classical
Morse code, which is developed by Samuel Morse when the telegraph was invented.
So, this was done using a mechanical device by clicking on a contact and it would produce
long and short clicks. So, the short clicks were called dots and the long clicks were called
dashes. We can as well think of them as representing the bits 0 and 1. So, in the Morse code encoding,
different letters do have different encodings. I mean English E is the most frequent letter and T is
another very frequent letter. So, Morse assign them codes of a dot that is 0 for E and a dash that is
1 for T. Then, Morse picked other frequent letters such as a and gave them two letter encoding.
So, a is encoded as dot dash or 0 1. Now, the problem with Morse's encoding is that it is ambiguous
when you come to decoding. So, for instance, if we look at the word the sequence 0 1,
then we do not know whether we should interpret each of these as a one letter code and get E T E T.
Or for instance, we should think of this as two two letter codes and get A A and so on.
So, depending on whether we stop at a 0 or extend 0 to 0 1, we can get many different interpretations.
Now, in practice in Morse code, what used to happen is that the operator gives a slight pause
indicating the end of the letter. So, therefore, effectively Morse code is not a binary code,
but it is a three letter code to 0 1 and pause. Now, when we are using of course, digital computers,
we do not want to go to three letters. So, we want to efficiently do this using just two letters.
So, in order to make a variable length code and unabiguously decodable, we need what is called
